documents.abstract: Independent technical commentary on the RESTORE melatonin trial (BMJ Open 2026;16:e107775; DOI 10.1136/bmjopen-2025-107775). The note examines the chronology of futility-rule prespecification, the reported intention-to-treat population and unavailable outcomes, and the interpretation of statistical power. The primary two-sided Fisher exact test is independently reproduced as P = 1.000 from the published aggregate counts. The documentary discrepancy requires dated protocol/SAP amendments and monitoring records; it does not establish outcome-driven stopping or invalid treatment results. Source-access limitations are stated explicitly. No participant-level reanalysis was performed. OpenAI ChatGPT assisted source checking, numerical verification, statistical interpretation, language editing, and preparation of the commentary. Responsibility rests with the named author.

Although agricultural extension methodologies have been widely studied, limited attention has been paid to the mismatch between field technicians’ methodological preferences and institutional constraints from a socio-technical systems perspective. This study analyzes rural extension methodologies in Latin America during 2022–2025, focusing on interactions among local and scientific knowledge, social actors, and territorial innovations. A qualitative, descriptive-documentary approach was adopted, incorporating comparative content analysis of 20 selected scientific publications and international reports on rural innovation systems. Evidence was extracted using structured multidimensional analytical matrices covering pedagogical, operational, and structural dimensions, then examined through comparative thematic analysis and theoretical triangulation. The reviewed evidence indicated a reported preference of 34.6% for individual extension methods, including farm visits, associated with their capacity to build mutual trust and support situated learning. It also identified a reported institutional mismatch of 28.4%, linked to rigid, top-down administrative regulations that constrain methodological choices. These findings challenge the assumption that individual extension is inherently hierarchical and highlight its pedagogical potential within agricultural innovation systems. The study contributes to agricultural innovation systems theory and the literature on socio-technical transitions by emphasizing the relationship between extension practices and institutional conditions. It concludes that methodological flexibility and socio-pedagogical competencies are important for extension agents and supports the design of adaptable, context-sensitive public advisory policies that accommodate diverse extension approaches.

Abstract This study examines changes in digital art’s creative mechanisms, subject relations, and conditions of existence through the lens of the philosophy of technology. Tracing the evolution from mechanical and electronic media to algorithmic systems, the paper argues that technology no longer functions merely as an external tool but increasingly intervenes in artistic cognition, creative processes, and the conditions under which works are generated. The paper outlines three notable dimensions of change in digital art: technologically mediated existence, distributed creative relations, and algorithmically shaped aesthetic processes. The paper also examines three tensions: Western aesthetic dominance via biased training data, NFT-driven value paradoxes, and destabilized artistic subjectivity under generative AI. Drawing on process philosophy, complexity theory, and technological phenomenology, it proposes a techno-cognitive framework positioning digital art as a dynamic interface between technology and human cognition. The study proposes evaluative and ethical discussion frameworks better suited to contemporary digital art, with the aim of supporting further theoretical analysis.

Abstract In the wake of terrible occurrences, social media has become the preferred source for real-time information. Social media has become a significant instrument for victims of catastrophes to express their needs, document incidents, request support and share information related to their situation. However, automated analysis may be fairly difficult in the case of casual, abbreviated, grammatically inconsistent, spelling-variant and other textual noisy communications. Artificial intelligence may be used to this data to enhance the response to catastrophes provided by technology and the well-being of humans and help in the improved detection and organization of communications related to disasters. The current research is a study on the feasibility of the use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) based on transformers to classify the social media postings about the tragedy with background noise. A social media dataset related to catastrophes is pre-processed adequately to develop classification models. For the comparison of the performance of the handling of textual content on catastrophes a transformer-based model and a conventional machine-learning baseline are taken into consideration. Some of the main performance indicators used to evaluate the models include accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. The problems caused by casual and distracting social media text are given specific attention. This project aims to (1) describe the challenges of collecting and evaluating noisy user-generated data and (2) empirically evaluate transformer-based text categorisation in a disaster-response setting. The research explores the use of AI-driven natural language processing on social media platforms connected to catastrophes to assist in the timely comprehension of crisis-related communication and human well-being. Moreover, it adds to the greater issue of Artificial Intelligence for social benefit.

The operating theatre is a complex high risk clinical environment that can create challenges to patient safety. Miscommunication, incorrect surgery/procedure on the wrong patient, medication errors, equipment issues, retained surgical items, physiological decline and delayed detection of complications can all cause issues to patient safety. Artificial intelligence is becoming an important tool within the operating theatre to improve patient safety by analysing large volumes of data.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is essential for modern cardiac diagnostics, yet it is difficult to access in remote areas. Remotely operated robotic-assisted ultrasound may enable access to services in rural and remote locations, while also improving ergonomics for the sonographer. This study evaluated the safety, usability and patient satisfaction of a novel robotic ultrasound assistance tool (RUAT). Methods: This open-label, single-site, single-arm clinical trial enrolled adult participants who had recently completed a standard manual echocardiogram. A trained sonographer performed a robot-assisted TTE from a dedicated workstation in the same room as the patient. Endpoints included safety measured by adverse events, technical and clinical usability, and patient satisfaction using surveys about the participants’ experience. Results: The trial cohort (n=30; mean age 62.9 ± 17.5 years; 70% men) all successfully completed the robot-assisted TTE and the patient satisfaction survey. There were no adverse events or adverse device effects. The functional verification checklist supporting technical usability demonstrated an average usability rate of 96.9% (95% CI [98.9–100.0]), with a 100% rate across 10 of 12 metrics. The sonographer’s review of the acquired robotic images measured the clinical usability and 29 of 30 examinations met acceptable diagnostic standards (96.7%; 95% CI [88.1–100.0]). The mean participant satisfaction score was 8.3 out of 10, with 96.7% scoring ≥6. Conclusion: The RUAT demonstrated high technical and clinical usability, as well as high acceptance by participants. These findings indicate that robot-assisted TTE is a viable strategy to enhance remote access to TTE services.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Oral cancer continues to be a significant health issue worldwide, and a late diagnosis is highly correlated with poorer treatment outcomes and shorter life expectancy. While these two steps (examining a patient and obtaining tissue cultures) are essential to this diagnosis (previously routine), they do not help to detect the patient in time at the population level. A minimally invasive, biological fluid such as saliva has many molecular components that may mirror pathological changes occurring in the oral cavity. Salivary omics domains could thereby yield a better assessment, through a combination of the domains, of the risk of oral cancer at an early stage. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further enhance the analysis of complex molecular patterns by integrating information from multiple salivary biomarker domains. Such approaches may support the identification of potential early indicators of oral cancer and improve the classification of individuals according to their estimated disease risk. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the potential of multi-omics salivary biomarkers (genomic/transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome) for the early detection and risk classification of oral cancer. The study also highlights the potential application of AI-based analytical approaches to integrate multi-omics biomarker information and clinical characteristics for improved oral cancer risk classification. Methods: The approach applied was quantitative cross-sectional and analytical, and involved a number of respondents of 279 people. Demographic and behavioural risk factors and the perception of being assessed for these risk factors by biomarkers were investigated, along with oral symptoms, clinical findings, and salivary multi-omics classifications. Normality test and Cronbach's Alpha reliability test, Bartlett's Test of Sphericity, and KMO Test, Independent Samples t test, One-Way Analysis of Variance, Kruskal-Wallis, Chi-Square Test of Independence, Pearson correlation and regression analysis were used in statistical analysis. Results: The results showed a good level of reliability with an average Cronbach's Alpha of 0.901 - 0.938. Supporting construct validity is the value of kmo which is excellent (0.959), and the Bartlett's test result shows that the p-value is less than 0.001. Gender difference, differences in age groups, differences in category of areca use and cooked chew (areca/users, non-users), differences in Betel chewing (areca, non-users) were the significant differences. The overall multi-omics risk classification was well correlated with the clinical examination status, χ² (9) = 429.967, p < 0.001. Overall multi-omics risk revealed significant associations between domains of major biomarkers, with the highest between clinical examination and overall multi-omics risk. The regression analysis resulted in a highly significant predictive model of overall risk classification (R = 0.943, R² = 0.889, p < 0.001), which explained a great variance of risk predictors that were included in the model. Conclusion: Results showed that the multi-omics biomarkers of saliva were a prevalent candidate for use as a minimally invasive tool to aid early detection/classification of OCD. Combination of use of molecular biomarker domains with clinical examination may lead to improved identification of patients likely to show symptoms of a clinical disorder that would warrant early diagnosis referral. The disease diagnosis performance needs to be further tested in other populations before the wide-scale application of the system. Future studies should investigate the integration of salivary multi-omics biomarkers using appropriately validated AI models, with particular attention to early cancer detection, risk classification, model interpretability, and external validation across independent populations.

Motorcycle workshop mechanics work in environments where vehicle exhaust may accumulate, particularly in workshops located near dense traffic and with limited ventilation. Carbon monoxide (CO) is not directly measured in this study; therefore, daily working hours and years of employment are used as occupational indicators of possible long-term exposure. This descriptive cross-sectional study analyzed serum creatinine levels among 30 motorcycle workshop mechanics on Jalan Riau, Pekanbaru. Respondents were selected by purposive sampling based on predefined eligibility criteria. Venous blood was collected, processed into serum, and analyzed using an Optiva photometer with a Glory Diagnostics enzymatic creatinine kit at 510 nm. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize creatinine distribution by age, daily working duration, and length of employment. The results showed that 17 respondents (56.67%) had serum creatinine levels above the reference range (>1.3 mg/dL), while 13 respondents (43.33%) had normal levels (0.7-1.3 mg/dL). Increased creatinine levels were more frequent among mechanics working 12 hours/day (75%) than among those working 8 hours/day (20%), and were also more common in respondents aged 30 years or older and those with more than 10 years of employment. These findings suggest that mechanics with longer occupational contact in CO-prone workshop environments may have a higher proportion of elevated serum creatinine. However, because ambient CO or carboxyhemoglobin was not measured, the results should be interpreted as an occupational-health screening finding rather than evidence of direct causality. Improved ventilation, routine health monitoring, and occupational safety education are recommended.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Biographies usually follow a life forward in time, and independent researchers who work outside institutions are rarely documented in a structured way. This article addresses the lack of critically labelled biographical accounts of independent artificial intelligence researchers by studying Satish Gajawada, a 2012 graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee whose fourteen years of independent work are distinguished by the coining of names for research fields, algorithms, a society, a title and a family of “theories of everything”. The purpose is to read this life through its vocabulary and to separate what has been named from what has been validated. The study uses a lexicon method: five source documents supplied by the subject were analysed, and seven terms were treated as biographical entries, each examined as an event, a method and a question for assessment. Every factual statement was labelled as documented, self-reported or interpretive. The principal results show a recurring “self and others” grammar that links philosophy to optimisation; an expanding programme of proposed fields; a large catalogue of themed swarm algorithms without reported comparative evaluation; a 2026 turn toward family-based ethics; and a growing practice of disclosure, including a small reproducible fairness test in which a penalty term reduced a demographic-parity gap from about 0.12 to 0.016 at a cost of about 1.9 percentage points of accuracy. The article concludes that the most defensible contribution is a consistent human-centred vocabulary for artificial intelligence, that adoption and independent validation remain unreported, and that the subject’s growing candour about the limits of his claims is the most significant recent development. Keywords: research ethics; artificial intelligence; biography; particle swarm optimisation; independent research; value-aligned artificial intelligence
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Rapid urbanization, increasing motorization, and spatial concentration ofemployment and services are putting increasing pressure on urban road networks. Trafficcongestion is not only a transportation problem, but also a multidimensional urbanplanning problem that affects travel time, economic productivity, energy consumption,air quality, road safety, and social amenity. This paper explores the relationship betweenroad infrastructure and traffic congestion, identifies the main mechanisms that causerecurrent and non-recurrent congestion, and systematizes engineering, planning, policy,and digital interventions. A literature-based analytical approach is used, combiningclassical theories of demand, network balance, and bottleneck effects with recentevidence on demand management policies, intelligent transportation systems (ITS),artificial intelligence, and integrated urban mobility. The analysis shows that increasingroad capacity alone cannot guarantee sustainable reductions in congestion, as additionalcapacity may encourage additional car traffic. Road network improvements are morelikely to achieve sustainable results when combined with adaptive traffic signalmanagement, public transport prioritization, parking and demand management,coordinated land-use planning, real-time information, and multimodal accessibility. Aconceptual framework is proposed that considers road capacity, traffic demand, networktopology, control quality, and passenger behavior as interacting variables. The paperconcludes with recommendations for developing cities, which are particularly relevantfor the rapidly developing urban centers of Central Asia.
